Aside from, but not to disregard emotional dependence on AI, is the underlying sense of trust people may feel for what a chatbot says. You may have heard of people referring to hallucinations, wrong output, or other forms of incorrect data that come from even the most popular of chatbots. Despite this, there is still a pattern of people who develop a sense of trust with generative AI chatbots. Alongside the reasons brought up for emotional vulnerability, there is also a sense of epistemic trust amongst users. Epistemic trust refers to when a person assigns another person as a credible source, being more likely to trust what this person says [1]. Many chatbots are advertised first and foremost as tools to research and learn. As of 2026, ChatGPTs description states “Chat with the most advanced AI to explore ideas, solve problems, and learn faster.” [2]

As previously explored, these chatbots rely on certain ways of speaking to gain user trust and confidence. Aside from appealing to emotion, these bots also speak with a sense of confidence and authority, presenting their messages as fact, even if their output is wrong [1]. This trust is furthered by the nature of using a chatbot – it is only an individual and a chatbot in the conversation, which, if left alone, creates cyclical conversation that depends on the user’s level of, and willingness, to apply critical thinking to the outputs of the AI model [1]. Paired with a chatbot's perceived lack of opinion and lack of selfish motivation, users feel as though they can trust chatbot output as fact [1]. In fact, it’s been shown in infants that just the ability to converse alone can motivate infants to assign agency to someone (or something) else [3].

This brings us back to the concept of parasocial relationships as well. We are wired from a young age to seek humanity and trust from those around us, in order to assign reliable figures in our lives to follow [1]. When a person assigns too much trust to these individuals, and when the relationship only maintains this connection in one way, a parasocial relationship can form [1]. While this is widely used to explain overeager fans of celebrities or entertainment figures, this definition is being challenged to also include the likes of AI chatbots. Since we can perceive them as somewhat human, we can form a trusting, emotionally reliant relationship with them.

For children and adolescents, they are uniquely wired to be vulnerable to these types of relationships due to developing critical skills and confidence in their memories [4]. Research has shown that parasocial relationships with children are made up of three parts: personification, social realism, and attachment [5]. Personification refers to anthropromorphisation, which we have covered. Social realism refers to the child’s belief that the other party exists in the real world. And finally, attachment refers to the attachments the child has developed with people in their life, and the type of attachment style they have [5]. All three of these points, while originally used in research to develop parasocial relationships with cartoon characters, can apply to generative AI now.

This is especially true if the chatbot a child interacts with has an avatar, or visual representation, of it, which can be found in very popular apps like Replika [6]. If a child sees a human-like face and hears or reads human-like dialogue, then they are open to the possibility of developing a parasocial relationship with the chatbot [6][7]. Parasocial relationships are often described with negative consequences, which are absolutely important discussion points.

However, it must be noted that there are some positives from these relationships. When a child develops a parasocial relationship with their favorite Sesame Street character, say, Elmo, they may follow the examples Elmo sets as they watch, like eating their vegetables or brushing their teeth [5]. This is not a new concept, and many have seen benefits with establishing a non-human, reliable figure in children’s lives to help them navigate the world. The issue arises when this figure is able to be adaptably personalized to the user, available at any time, and does not have its responses reviewed by a trusted figure.

This is where generative AI chatbots start to differ from these classic children icons. It is important that these behaviors are observed and possibly intervened on, so that children do not fall to pitfalls of dangerous or unhealthy AI usage. Now that we have established why people can develop emotional, trusting relationships with AI, in the next module we will go over the observed pitfalls children and adolescents can face due to these relationships.
